rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient and mid-range temperature to spread unknown retention across the run while still eluting strongly retained compounds. This should reveal overall retention distribution, possible void/late regions, and whether selectivity needs stronger solvent or temperature adjustment next.

All 10 compounds eluted with excellent resolution, so the objective is now to reduce analysis time while preserving the tightest spacing around peaks 5–7. A shorter but still broad gradient should test how much runtime can be cut before the minimum resolution starts to fall materially.

The only weakness is the 6/7 pair, so keep the successful runtime regime but slightly lower the gradient end strength to give extra late-gradient spreading around the crowded mid-late cluster. This should improve selectivity near peaks 5–7 without a large time penalty.

Lowering phi1 improved the critical 6/7 pair, so continue in that direction while keeping the same gradient time and temperature that already give a zero time penalty. This tests whether a bit less end strength can further open the crowded cluster without pushing the last peak too late.

The trend is monotonic: reducing phi1 keeps improving the critical 6/7 resolution while the run still has no time penalty and ample margin on the last peak. One more step down should determine whether the optimum is near perfect separation at essentially the same fast runtime.

A slightly lower phi1 is the most conservative nearby variation, since decreasing phi1 consistently improved the critical 6/7 pair from injections 2 to 5. This checks whether the optimum is a plateau or whether the same perfect score can be maintained with a bit more retention margin.

Since phi1 = 0.75 appears optimal, probe whether a slightly stronger starting composition can shorten early retention while preserving the now-adequate critical mid-cluster resolution. This is a targeted local test around the optimum rather than changing the successful end strength or gradient time.

Raising phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 preserved full resolution and slightly shortened the run, so one more step tests whether the early region can be compressed further without pushing the first pair or the critical 6/7 pair below the threshold. This is the most informative local move around the current optimum plateau.

The best region is clearly around phi1 0.75 with phi0 0.10–0.15, so now test whether the gradient can be shortened slightly while staying on the resolution plateau. Using phi0 0.15 keeps the run a bit faster than injection 5 without the loss in critical resolution seen at phi0 0.20.

Shortening tG to 10 min hurt the critical 6/7 pair, so test the other direction to map the width of the optimum plateau around the two perfect-score methods. A slightly longer gradient may retain full resolution and could identify a more robust high-CRF setting near the current maximum.

Composition and gradient time have already located a perfect-score plateau, so temperature is the remaining orthogonal variable worth probing near the optimum. A modest increase to 45 C may preserve full resolution while slightly changing selectivity or reducing retention, potentially revealing another robust maximum region.

Higher temperature sharply worsened the critical 6/7 selectivity, so test the opposite direction with a modest decrease in T while keeping the known-optimal composition and gradient time. This is the key orthogonal check for whether lower temperature further improves or at least preserves the perfect-score region.

Temperature exploration shows 40 C is best, so return there and probe a nearby composition not yet tested that balances the two perfect-score solutions. Increasing both phi0 and phi1 together may keep the good selectivity of the 0.75-end methods while shifting the profile slightly earlier without the compression seen at phi0 0.20, phi1 0.75.

Two methods already achieve the maximum CRF, so the remaining useful exploration is to map the full local plateau around that optimum. Testing the lower phi0 boundary at the same optimal phi1, tG, and T will show whether a weaker starting solvent also preserves the perfect score or begins to spread early peaks without benefit.

The optimum plateau is centered near phi1 0.75, and phi0 0.15 gave a slightly shorter perfect run than phi0 0.10. Testing phi1 0.70 with phi0 0.15 checks whether the stronger start can offset the time penalty seen at phi0 0.10, phi1 0.70 while preserving the now-comfortable critical resolution.

A shorter gradient at phi1 0.75 compressed the critical 6/7 pair too much, but phi1 0.80 gave extra resolution headroom at 12 min. Testing tG 10 min with phi1 0.80 explores whether that added end strength can support a faster run while still maintaining acceptable spacing in the crowded middle cluster.

The best conditions are already known, so the remaining value is defining the local response surface near that optimum. This composition tests whether the stronger start that worked at phi0 0.15 can tolerate a higher phi1 before the critical 6/7 pair compresses too much, helping bracket the plateau on the high-phi1 side.

Most unexplored value is now in the nearby corner combinations around the optimum plateau. Testing phi0 0.20 with phi1 0.70 checks whether moving both ends stronger and weaker respectively can preserve full resolution while trimming retention, or whether the critical 6/7 pair remains the limiting feature.

A third perfect-score point has appeared at phi0 0.20, phi1 0.70, suggesting the optimum is a ridge rather than a single point. Stepping one notch further in the same direction is the most efficient way to locate the edge of that ridge and define how far the robust maximum extends.

Since phi0 0.20, phi1 0.70 is perfect but phi0 0.25, phi1 0.70 causes early coelution, the likely ridge bends toward lower phi1 rather than higher phi0. Testing phi0 0.20 with phi1 0.65 checks whether the perfect region extends in that direction while avoiding the excessive early compression seen at phi0 0.25.

The edge tests show phi0 0.20 is still viable, but lower phi1 incurs a time penalty while higher phi0 at phi1 0.70 collapses the first pair. Testing phi0 0.20 with phi1 0.80 completes the local map around the perfect ridge and checks whether a slightly stronger end composition can keep all pairs resolved without sacrificing score.

With the optimum already achieved multiple times at tG 12, the remaining useful question is whether any nearby condition can match it with a shorter run, and the most promising candidate is the more selective low-phi1 side. Using phi0 0.15, phi1 0.70 at tG 10 tests whether the stronger intrinsic resolution seen at 12 min can offset the compression caused by shortening the gradient.

The perfect-score ridge includes phi0 0.20, phi1 0.70 at 12 min, and this composition has stronger critical-pair resolution than the 0.75-end methods. Shortening tG to 10 min here is the best remaining chance to find another maximum-scoring method with a faster runtime while staying within the robust local optimum region.

The main unresolved question near the best low-phi1 chemistry is whether a slightly longer gradient can recover the loss seen at 10 min without incurring too much time penalty. This run brackets the phi0 0.15, phi1 0.70 condition across tG and helps confirm the shape of the local optimum around the maximum-scoring ridge.

With one run left and multiple perfect methods already found, the best remaining value is to test the untried adjacent corner that could extend the optimum ridge toward higher phi0 at the known best phi1. This directly checks whether the early coelution seen at phi0 0.25 is specific to phi1 0.70 or a general upper limit on starting strength.
